strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem for speech language models: obtaining good reconstruction quality with fewer acoustic codebooks. Evaluating both autoregressive VALL-E and parallel MobileSpeech connects the codec contribution to downstream language modeling.

The reconstruction evaluation covers three datasets, several codec families, and complementary metrics. The four-codebook system shows promising improvements: on LibriTTS Test-Clean, PESQ increases from 2.4026 with Vocos to 2.6329, and STOI increases from 0.9231 to 0.9375.

Downstream results provide evidence of practical utility. Speaker similarity improves over Encodec+Vocos for both TTS architectures while WER remains comparable. Human evaluation includes 50 samples with at least ten ratings per sample and distinguishes quality, prosody, and speaker similarity.

The manuscript reports dataset sources, preprocessing, optimization settings, and hardware, and provides a link described as containing code and pretrained models. These are useful foundations for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central contribution is not isolated experimentally. Section 4.5 compares pretrained Encodec/Vocos systems with a model that changes quantization, training data, and end-to-end optimization simultaneously. This cannot establish that MCRVQ causes the improvements. A standard-RVQ control trained with the same data, decoder, and optimization budget is needed to support the mechanism claim.

The claimed reduction in the gap between acoustic tokens and language modeling remains largely motivational. There is no measurement of information distribution across codebooks, text-conditioned token predictability, or downstream computational savings. The downstream table does not identify the codebook counts used. Better reconstructed audio and speaker similarity alone do not establish that the first channel becomes easier to model.

Important implementation details remain ambiguous. Section 3.3 and Equation 5 do not clearly specify channel-specific masks, their inference behavior, or cumulative residual updates. Codebook sizes, loss weights, decoder dimensions, and several downstream settings are missing. The 20,000 hours of internal Chinese data also limit independent training replication; more precise data composition and a reproducible public-data configuration would help.

The reported results contain an unresolved inconsistency: Table 3 gives Language-Codec LJSpeech UTMOS scores of 3.7091 and 3.8955, whereas Table 4 reports 3.8549 and 4.0127 for the corresponding configurations. Claims of broad superiority also exceed the tables: SpeechTokenizer has higher UTMOS in several settings, and other codecs lead on some fidelity and speaker metrics. The discrepancy needs correction, and conclusions should describe the observed tradeoffs.

The statistical support for downstream improvements is incomplete. Relative to Encodec+Vocos, several MOS gains are small compared with the reported uncertainty, whose meaning and calculation are unspecified. Paired significance analysis and uncertainty for objective improvements would clarify which gains are reliable. Overlapping intervals do not establish equivalence, but the presented evidence does not establish consistent superiority either.

Comparisons omit particularly relevant alternatives: HiFi-Codec targets reconstruction with fewer quantizers, and SpeechTokenizer directly addresses language-model-compatible representations but is absent from downstream evaluation. All evaluation corpora are English read speech, limiting support for the multilingual and real-world generalization motivation. The empirical promise is sufficient to justify revision, but the unresolved attribution, specification, and reporting issues prevent a sound Findings recommendation in the current version.
